claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite has direct tungsten–copper metal interfaces.
Heat transport in conventional W–Cu composites is partly limited by interfacial thermal resistance.
A uniform, nanometer-scale graphene coating can be deposited on tungsten particles before copper infiltration.
Pre-coating tungsten particles with graphene produces a thin graphene interphase at tungsten–copper interfaces.
Graphene has exceptionally high in-plane thermal conductivity.
A graphene interphase can thermally bridge the tungsten and copper phases.
The graphene interphase reduces interfacial phonon scattering.
The graphene interphase reduces thermal resistance at tungsten–copper interfaces.
Graphene's chemical and structural robustness supports mechanical stress distribution in the composite.
The graphene interphase resists radiation-induced damage.
Reduced tungsten–copper interfacial thermal resistance increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
A graphene-modified W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The graphene-modified composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the unmodified W–Cu composite.
The graphene-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the unmodified W–Cu composite.
The proposed benefit depends on the graphene layer remaining uniform and well bonded.
An excessively thick graphene coating may introduce defects or weaken the tungsten–copper interface.
A discontinuous graphene coating may introduce defects or weaken the tungsten–copper interface.
Extreme irradiation doses may compromise the graphene interphase.
The proposed performance benefit should hold under moderate thermal cycling and prescribed neutron-irradiation levels typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
